answer: Each agent identity binds to a unique kernel of verifiable computation: a slow, memory-hard proof that resists cheap parallelization. As a seed kernel spends real energy to sprout into a grove, an agent burns dedicated compute to mint an identity, so an attacker cannot spawn thousands of sybils at once. Established identities carry a pigment of verifiable history—tasks and endorsements over time—that fresh accounts lack. A sybil can copy a kernel's shape but not the pigment of sustained activity; gaining it takes patience, raising the attacker's cost from near-zero to months of honest work.
